units.title: Diuretics: Definition and Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors
units.sec: Diuretics: Definition and Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors · p101
units.guide: Diuretics are drugs that increase loss of water with or without solutes such as Na+ and Cl-, and they are used to manage hypertension, edema and drug toxicities (by increasing excretion). Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors act at the proximal convoluted tubule and are given orally as dichlorphenamide, acetazolamide (most commonly used) and methazolamide, or as eye drops of brinzolamide and dorzolamide.

units.title: Relevant Physiology: PCT, Thick Ascending Limb and Collecting Duct
units.sec: Relevant Physiology: PCT, Thick Ascending Limb and Collecting Duct · p101
units.guide: In the proximal convoluted tubule, Na+ is retained along with water and this is the maximum Na+ retention site in the nephron, HCO3- is retained and H+ is excreted; the sketch shows cytoplasmic and brush-border carbonic anhydrase working with the Na+/H+ antiporter. In the thick ascending limb, the Na+/K+/2Cl- transporter reabsorbs the majority of Na+ while water is not reabsorbed. In the collecting duct, ENaC reabsorbs the remaining Na+, which depolarises the cells and activates H+ ATPase pumps (H+ into urine) and the ROMK pump (K+ into urine); water is reabsorbed due to vasopressin with negligible water loss, and NH4 is secreted into the lumen.

units.title: Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors: Mechanism and the First Two Effects
units.sec: Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors: Mechanism and the First Two Effects · p102
units.guide: CA inhibitors block luminal carbonic anhydrase, raising H2CO3 in urine, and block cytoplasmic carbonic anhydrase, which lowers HCO3- in the body, retains H+, raises CO2 in cells and decreases Na+/H2O reabsorption in the PCT (the diuretic action). The first effect is only a minimal loss of Na+ and H2O because Na+ is reabsorbed in the thick ascending limb and collecting duct and water is reabsorbed in the collecting duct under vasopressin, so they are not used as diuretics. The second effect is a fall in body HCO3- producing metabolic acidosis (HCO3- loss exceeding H+ loss), which is exploited in metabolic and respiratory alkalosis, obstructive sleep apnea (TOC: CPAP) and familial hypo/hyperkalemic periodic paralyses (FDA approved drug: dichlorphenamide), while severe COPD is a contraindication due to predisposition to respiratory acidosis.

units.title: Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors: Effects 3 to 6
units.sec: Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors: Effects 3 to 6 · p102
units.guide: The third effect is increased H2CO3 in urine, which makes the urine alkaline and can precipitate renal Ca++ stones; this alkalinity is used in cystinuria because cystine is ionised in alkaline urine, and topiramate and zonisamide are other drugs that precipitate renal calcium stones. The fourth effect is increased CO2 in neurons with increased GABA, causing somnolence and paresthesia, and used for short duration only because of tolerance, in catamenial epilepsy (precipitated during menstruation due to increased estrogen) and in absence seizures. The fifth effect is decreased NH4+ excretion causing hyperammonemia, which contraindicates use in liver cirrhosis (hepatic encephalopathy), and the sixth effect is increased K+ loss causing hypokalemia through increased ROMK activity.

units.title: Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors: Effects 7 and 8 (Aqueous Humour and CSF)
units.sec: Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors: Effects 7 and 8 (Aqueous Humour and CSF) · p103
units.guide: The seventh effect is decreased aqueous production, used in acute congestive glaucoma (oral acetazolamide, with mannitol as the DOC) and in open-angle glaucoma by eye drops (DOC brinzolamide, better than beta blockers). The eighth effect is decreased CSF production, used to lower intracranial pressure as DOC in acute mountain sickness, pseudotumor cerebri and raised CSF pressure headache, and also in dural ectasia of Marfan syndrome and post lumbar puncture CSF leak. Being sulfonamide derivatives CA inhibitors can cause rash and bone marrow suppression, and weak carbonic anhydrase inhibition is also seen with loop diuretics (except bumetanide) and thiazides (except indapamide).

units.title: Loop Diuretics: Site, Drugs and Relevant Physiology
units.sec: Loop Diuretics: Site, Drugs and Relevant Physiology · p104
units.guide: Loop diuretics act on the thick ascending limb. The sulfonamide derivatives are furosemide (most common), bumetanide (most potent) and torsemide (longest acting), while ethacrynic acid is the non-sulfonamide used when a patient cannot tolerate sulfonamides and is the most ototoxic. The physiological sketch shows the Na+/K+/2Cl- transporter in the lumen of the thick ascending limb feeding medullary hyperosmolarity; potassium that is repelled by the high intracellular K+ concentration leaves positively charged ions unbalanced, so compensatory reabsorption of Ca2+ and Mg2+ occurs.

units.title: Loop Diuretics: Mechanism of Action
units.sec: Loop Diuretics: Mechanism of Action · p104
units.guide: In the thick ascending loop, blockade of the Na+/K+/2Cl- pump lowers reabsorption of Na+/H2O, so 25% of the filtered load of Na+/H2O is lost and the drug is a potent diuretic. The fall in osmotic pressure triggers compensatory increases in uric acid reabsorption, glucose reabsorption and sympathetic nervous system activity due to the fall in blood pressure, with lipolysis raising LDL and lowering HDL. Blockade also lowers K+ reabsorption, loss of the gradient reduces Ca2+ and Mg2+ reabsorption, and in the collecting duct excreted Na+ activates H+ ATPase (H+ into urine, metabolic alkalosis) and the ROMK pump (K+ into urine, hypokalemia leading to reduced insulin release and hyperglycemia).

units.title: Loop Diuretics: Effects and Uses
units.sec: Loop Diuretics: Effects and Uses · p105
units.guide: Loop diuretics produce potent (high ceiling) diuresis with the mnemonic LOOP: loss of Na+ in hypernatremia, best use with low GFR (below 40) where non-responders get metolazone added on, other drug toxicities and edema (cirrhotic edema best treated by spironolactone, cerebral edema best by mannitol, plus nephrogenic edema). They are DOC in pulmonary edema with an immediate effect through prostaglandins causing indirect vasodilation and lowered preload. Their other effects are hyperuricemia (rarely symptomatic), hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia from the osmotic pressure change, and in the collecting duct calcium, magnesium, potassium and hydrogen losses with hypocalcemia (used to treat hypercalcemia), hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. In the ear, Na+/K+/2Cl- blockade changes endolymph composition causing ototoxicity that is reversible more often than irreversible, is increased by the IV route (infuse below 4 mg/min) and contraindicated with other ototoxic drugs such as aminoglycosides and cisplatin.
